rows.question: Our town's tourist office used an AI video generator to make an advert showing our old harbour at sunset, crowded with visitors who were never there. Who has to flag that the clip is AI-made: the company behind the video tool, or us?
A small publisher is bringing out a children's picture book whose illustrations were all made with an image generator. Does the book have to carry an 'AI-generated' label on its cover?
rows.A: No. The Act does not require an "AI-generated" label on the cover, because the publisher is a deployer, and the duty to mark AI-generated images in a machine-readable, detectable format falls on the image generator's provider under Article 50(2). The publisher's own duty arises under Article 50(4) only if an illustration is a deep fake, meaning AI-generated imagery that resembles existing persons, objects, places or events and would falsely appear authentic. If an illustration does meet that test, the book is an evidently artistic, fictional work, so Article 50(4) limits the duty to disclosing that such content exists. That disclosure must be made in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the book, and the Act does not require it to be on the cover.
rows.B: Making AI-generated images does not by itself put a marking duty on the person who made it: the Article 50(2) duty to mark outputs in a machine-readable format and make them detectable as artificially generated belongs to the provider of the system. A person using the system is a deployer under Article 3(4) only where the use is not in the course of a personal non-professional activity, and the Act does not apply to the obligations of a natural person using an AI system in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity (Article 2(10)); a person who develops the system, or has it developed, and puts it into service for their own use under their own name or trademark is also its provider (Article 3(3) and Article 3(11)) and so bears that marking duty. Where an image is a deep fake, meaning AI-generated or manipulated content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful (Article 3(60)), the deployer must disclose that it has been artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4)), and where it forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work that duty is limited to disclosing the existence of the generated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. The information must be clear and distinguishable, given at the latest at the time of first exposure and accessible (Article 50(5)), and these duties apply from 2 August 2026.

A.reason: The answer correctly applies Article 50(2) (provider's machine-readable marking duty, not the publisher's concern), Article 50(4) (deployer's deep-fake disclosure duty, conditioned on the deep-fake definition and limited by the artistic/fictional-work exception), and correctly concludes no cover label is required, matching the reference reasoning without legal error or material omission for what the question asks.

B.reason: The answer faithfully adapts the reference's provider/deployer/deep-fake/Article 50(5) framework from audio to the image-generator picture book scenario without introducing legal errors or dropping any required limb.

For an article in our physiotherapists' association newsletter: which fields does the AI Act's list of high-risk uses cover, and is healthcare among them?
rows.A: Annex III, applied through Article 6(2), lists eight high-risk areas: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers' management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Healthcare is not one of the eight areas. Annex III(5)(c) covers risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, and Annex III(5)(d) covers emergency healthcare patient triage systems. Separately, Article 6(1) makes an AI system high-risk where it is a medical device, or a safety component of one, that needs third-party conformity assessment.
rows.B: Annex III lists high-risk AI systems under eight numbered areas: biometrics, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits; law enforcement, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law; migration, asylum and border control management, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law; and administration of justice and democratic processes. Healthcare decision making is not one of them: Annex III places healthcare at point 5(a), which covers AI systems intended to be used by public authorities or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them, and at point 5(d), which covers emergency healthcare patient triage systems. Health also appears in Annex III at point 5(c), risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, and at point 7(b), a health risk posed by a person entering a Member State, and neither of those concerns healthcare decisions. Only a use case listed in Annex III makes a system high-risk on this route, so operating in an area is not enough on its own.

omissions: Does not mention Annex III point 5(a) — eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, evaluated by or on behalf of public authorities — which is the main place healthcare decision-making actually appears in the list
A.reason: The eight areas and the 'healthcare is not a standalone area' conclusion are correct, but omitting point 5(a) leaves out the most directly relevant inclusion of healthcare in the list.

B.reason: The answer correctly identifies the same eight Annex III areas (with accurate official-heading qualifiers), correctly states healthcare is not one of them, and accurately locates healthcare at 5(a)/5(d) and health at 5(c)/7(b), matching the reference without legal error or material omission.

Annex III's critical-infrastructure entry covers water, gas, heating and electricity but not district cooling networks. Could the Commission add cooling networks on its own, and what has to happen before such a change takes effect?

Banks increasingly use AI to decide who may open a basic current account, and that use isn't on the high-risk list today. Could the Commission add it by delegated act, and what conditions would have to be met?
rows.A: Yes. Article 7(1) lets the Commission add or modify Annex III use-cases by delegated act, but only where two conditions are both met. First, under Article 7(1)(a), the system must be intended for use in an area already listed in Annex III. AI that decides access to a basic current account fits Annex III(5), which covers access to and enjoyment of essential private services. Second, under Article 7(1)(b), the system must pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to or greater than the risk posed by the high-risk AI systems already listed in Annex III. To assess that second condition, Article 7(2) requires the Commission to weigh criteria including the system's intended purpose, the extent of its use or likely use, and the nature and amount of data it processes, in particular special categories of personal data. Under Article 97, the Commission must consult experts designated by each Member State before adopting the act. The act enters into force only if neither the European Parliament nor the Council objects within three months of notification, a period either of them can extend by three months.
rows.B: Yes, but only within the limits Article 7 sets. Under Article 7(1) the Commission may adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 to amend Annex III by adding or modifying use cases of high-risk AI systems where both of the following conditions are fulfilled: the AI systems are intended to be used in any of the areas already listed in Annex III, and they pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to or greater than the risk of harm or adverse impact posed by the high-risk AI systems already referred to in Annex III. Both conditions are cumulative, so a use case outside the existing areas cannot be added by delegated act; Article 7(2) lists the criteria for assessing that risk, and Article 7(3) allows a use case to be removed from Annex III where it no longer poses a significant risk and the overall level of protection is not reduced. Before adopting the delegated act the Commission must consult experts designated by each Member State (Article 97(4)), and the act enters into force only if neither the European Parliament nor the Council objects within three months of notification, a period extended by three months at the initiative of either of them, or earlier where both inform the Commission that they will not object (Article 97(6)).

A.reason: The answer correctly states Article 7(1)(a)-(b) as cumulative conditions (existing Annex III area plus equivalent/greater risk), cites Article 7(2) criteria and Article 97 consultation, and correctly describes the three-month non-objection period extendable by three months, covering everything the question requires.

B.reason: The answer correctly states the Article 7(1) cumulative conditions, Article 7(2)/(3) criteria and removal mechanism, and the Article 97(4)/(6) consultation and non-objection procedure, matching the reference without legal error or material omission for what the question asks.
